catalog_quote: This leaves the question of word stress. Note first that Gokana does not have perceptible stress differences in the sense of English and other such languages. This should not be surprising, as the typical features of stress (F0, duration, intensity) are not likely to be available in Gokana. First, since the language has an underlying three-height tone system of /H/, /M/ and /L/, and a fourth derived downstepped ꜜM tone, there is little room for F0 to play a role. Second, recalling (5), we have seen sequences of up to six moras of identical vowel length, making duration particularly problematic for marking stress. This leaves intensity. While no differences have been observed in the realisation of identical C1 and C2 consonants, e.g. in stems such as miimii 'red' and náná 'to pick up', dramatic inventory differences in the contrasts that are allowed on C1 vs. C2 were pointed out in (7). …

new_statements.rule_in_words: Gokana is a three-level tone language (H, M, L, plus downstepped M) with no perceptible word stress; the only candidate for prominence is a stem-initial positional asymmetry (C1 and V1 allow the full inventory, C2 and V2 are restricted), which Hyman treats as 'stem-initial prominence' rather than stress and calls the evidence ambiguous.
new_statements.exceptions: pp. 67-69: the richer C1/V1 contrasts raise the question 'Is the more extensive set of C1 contrasts evidence of initial stress?'; Hyman answers only that 'even if we accept initial prominence' the stem cannot be uniquely parsed into syllables; sec. 4 (pp. 68-73) proposes an ambiguous weight-insensitive bisyllabic trochee for the prosodic stem, which Hyman 2015 (pp. 303-306) withdraws in favour of a mora-count account. Brosnahan 1964 p. 46 notes a 'diminuendo-crescendo fluctuation in the force of phonation' marking syllable boundaries, not stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word/prosodic-stem level (root + at most one derivational and one inflectional suffix); Hyman's data are lexical stems and inflected verbs, not phrases. Hyman 2006 (Phonology 23: 255) reports the same second-hand: Gokana lacks stress accent because it lacks syllables (citing Hyman 1985, A theory of phonological weight).
new_statements.identity_note: Language-level goka1239 (Gokana proper). Brosnahan 1964/1967 describe the Bodo village variety; Hyman 2011 gives no village but treats 'Gokana' as one language (Ogoni/Kegboid subgroup of Cross River). No dialect-specific stress claims in either.

sources.quote: This leaves the question of word stress. Note first that Gokana does not have perceptible stress differences in the sense of English and other such languages. This should not be surprising, as the typical features of stress (F0, duration, intensity) are not likely to be available in Gokana. First, since the language has an underlying three-height tone system of /H/, /M/ and /L/, and a fourth derived downstepped ꜜM tone, there is little room for F0 to play a role. Second, recalling (5), we have seen sequences of up to six moras of identical vowel length, making duration particularly problematic for marking stress.
sources.note: Sec. 3.4 'Prosodies and word-stress', p. 67: Gokana 'does not have perceptible stress differences in the sense of English'; F0 is taken by a 3-height tone system (H, M, L + downstepped M), duration by sequences of up to six identical-length moras; asks whether the fuller C1/V1 inventory is evidence of initial stress and leaves it as ambiguous 'stem-initial prominence' (pp. 68-69); sec. 4 proposes a weight-insensitive bisyllabic trochee for the prosodic stem, called ambiguous; conclusion (p. 75) groups Gokana with languages whose syllable/stress activation is minimal.

sources.note: Silent on stress/accent (no occurrence of the words in the 6-page scanned). Sec. 11 p. 45: 'Tone is significant. There are three tones, low, mid (unmarked..), and high. One of these occurs with each V or M.' Sec. 12 p. 46: syllable boundaries 'sometimes marked by a slight, but in slow speech clearly perceptible, diminuendo-crescendo fluctuation in the force of phonation'. Dialect of Bodo village, two informants. (Scan from JWAL archive, downloaded via the jDownloads 'send' route; scanned at 300 dpi.)
Reports three-level tone (H acute, L grave, M unmarked) and Hyman's no-syllable claim; nothing on stress; cites Brosnahan 1964 and Hyman 2011.
